title: Lesson 24: Failure Post-Mortem: When a Workflow Died, What You Do Next
description: Running a blameless post-mortem on a dead workflow: what a post-mortem is, how to separate the symptom from the root cause with five whys, and how to turn a failure into action items that prevent recurrence.

questions.question: Marcus's weekly client report workflow ran on Friday at 5pm, showed no error, but produced no report. His first instinct was to re-run it. Per the lesson, why should he resist that instinct and start a post-mortem instead?
options: Re-running a dead workflow without understanding why it died tells him almost nothing: if it works on the re-run he has a working workflow and no idea what broke it, so it will break again
Re-running a workflow is always forbidden, because any re-run corrupts the run log and makes the failure impossible to diagnose
Re-running a workflow is pointless because a workflow that fails once will always fail, so he should abandon it entirely
Re-running a workflow is only useful if he changes the prompt first, since the failure is always caused by the instructions
questions.explanation: The lesson says Marcus's first instinct to re-run is worth resisting, because re-running a dead workflow without understanding why it died tells him almost nothing: if it works on the re-run he has a working workflow and no idea what broke it, which means it will break again. The post-mortem starts before the re-run, with the question of what actually happened.

questions.question: Marcus's five-whys analysis ended with the finding that his workflow had no check for empty input, so an empty data read looked like a normal run. Per the lesson, what is the root cause of the failure?
options: The missing check for empty input, because it is the underlying condition Marcus can actually fix, while the format change is only the proximate cause he cannot fully control
The data source's format change, because that is the immediate trigger that happened right before the failure
The email step, because the report never reached the client's inbox
Marcus's carelessness in building the workflow, because a better builder would have predicted the format change
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes proximate cause from root cause: the format change is the proximate cause, the immediate trigger Marcus could not have predicted and cannot fully control, while the missing check for empty input is the root cause, the underlying condition he can fix today. The five whys exist to reach the root cause, not stop at the proximate one.

questions.question: After running his post-mortem, Marcus wrote two action items: add a check that fails loudly on empty input, and add the data source's format to his runbook. Per the lesson, why are these action items the point of the whole exercise?
options: A post-mortem with no action items is a story, not a fix, because the follow-up actions with owners and deadlines are what prevent the failure from recurring
Action items are optional, since the real value of a post-mortem is the timeline that documents what happened
Action items only matter for team workflows, because a solo workflow owner does not need to track fixes
Action items should be written but never assigned, since assigning them creates blame
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that a post-mortem that ends with conclusions but no one assigned to act on them is a report, not a fix, and that the follow-up actions are the point. Google's SRE team treats the preventive actions as the measure of a post-mortem's worth. Action items with owners and deadlines are what turn a dead workflow into a lesson.
